# Loading vectors fast

Binary `COPY` loaded 50,000 rows of 384-dimension vectors in 0.56 s, twenty times faster than the
11.5 s the ORM took, because it sends each vector in pgvector's own binary format. Text `COPY` turns
every float into text and back, and pgpq pays for a Postgres array on the way. The same
holds in reverse, where binary `COPY` reads the table back into numpy faster than the alternatives.

## Loading 50,000 vectors

```
    method   | seconds | rows/s |  MB/s | vs orm
-------------+---------+--------+-------+--------
 orm         |    11.5 |   4347 |   6.7 | 1.0x
 executemany |     8.3 |   6024 |   9.3 | 1.4x
 copy_text   |     6.8 |   7358 |  11.3 | 1.7x
 copy_binary |    0.56 |  89363 | 137.3 | 20.6x
 pgpq        |    1.32 |  37746 |  58.0 | 8.7x
```

The rows in the table are these methods, in order:

- `session.add_all(...)` through the ORM, which is what the app's ingest does and is fine for
  hundreds of rows
- Core `insert()` with a list of dicts, which uses the driver's `executemany` and does a little better
- `COPY` in text format, which prints every float as text and parses it again on the server
- `COPY ... (FORMAT BINARY)` with pgvector's binary dumper, which sends floats as floats
- [pgpq](https://github.com/adriangb/pgpq), which goes from Parquet to Arrow to the Postgres binary
  format, with rows landing in a `FLOAT4[]` staging table because pgpq has no `vector` type

The staging table is why pgpq loses to plain binary `COPY`, even before an `INSERT ... SELECT` casts
the rows. On the wire, a Postgres array puts a 4-byte length in front of every element, so a
`FLOAT4[]` takes twice the bytes of a `vector`.

Binary `COPY` needs one call to teach psycopg the `vector` type, and then it writes one row at a
time:

```python
from pgvector.psycopg import register_vector

register_vector(conn)  # teaches psycopg the vector type, binary dumper included
with conn.cursor() as cur, cur.copy("COPY items (title, embedding) FROM STDIN (FORMAT BINARY)") as copy:
    copy.set_types(["text", "vector"])
    for title, vec in rows:  # vec: a numpy float32 array
        copy.write_row((title, vec))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Build the index after loading

Build the HNSW index once the table is loaded. Maintaining it row by row during a load costs more
than one build over the finished table.
:::

## Reading back, binary COPY wins again

The lab read the same table back as an `(n, 384)` numpy array in three ways:

```
 read back as numpy | seconds | rows/s |  MB/s | vs psycopg_rows
--------------------+---------+--------+-------+-----------------
 psycopg_rows       |    0.53 |  95004 | 145.9 | 1.0x
 copy_binary        |     0.4 | 125512 | 192.8 | 1.3x
 adbc_arrow         |    0.74 |  67889 | 104.3 | 0.7x
```

Binary `COPY ... TO STDOUT`, decoded in one numpy pass, is the fastest. [ADBC](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/)
does not know `vector` either, so the query casts to `real[]`, which arrives as `list<float>` and
pays the array overhead again. ADBC is still the one to use when the destination is Arrow anyway, as
with Polars, DuckDB or Parquet.

::: {.chapter-notebook}
The comparison runs from `src/examples/bench/pg_copy.py`, and `src/vecio.py` keeps the binary decoder
and the ADBC reader for reuse.
:::
